title: When the Power Goes Out, the Fridge Has a Clock
subtitle: A calm, shared plan can help you protect food before, during and after a blackout.
imageAlt: Two friends check a refrigerator thermometer and place a cooler beside the kitchen counter during a power outage.
imageConcept: A warmly lit home kitchen at dusk: two friends stand together beside a closed refrigerator, one holding a small appliance thermometer and the other setting out a cooler and frozen gel packs.
body: The clock starts when the power stops

A blackout can turn ordinary food decisions into a guessing game: Is the milk still cold? Should the freezer door be opened to check? A few decisions made in advance can replace guesswork with a plan. The essential move during an outage is simple: keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed. A closed refrigerator can keep food safe for up to four hours; a full freezer for about 48 hours, or a half-full freezer for about 24 hours, according to the CDC. Those are planning windows, not guarantees that every item is safe afterward. The refrigerator’s temperature, how long power was out and the type of food all matter. [1]

The aim is not to predict every emergency. It is to make the first steps easy to find and share, especially if the person who usually manages the kitchen is away, tired or dealing with other urgent needs.
Make the useful things easy to find

Before an outage, check whether the refrigerator and freezer have appliance thermometers and whether the refrigerator is at 40°F or below. The thermometers help you make a more informed assessment later; they are not a reason to open the doors repeatedly during the outage. Keep a cooler and frozen gel packs somewhere accessible, rather than buried behind seasonal supplies. USDA recommends keeping cooler food at 40°F or below. [3]

Take a minute to identify where the cooler, packs and thermometer are, and decide who can reach them. If several people share the home, put the information where they can find it without needing to ask one person. A short note on the refrigerator or in a shared phone note can say where the supplies are, where to find current food-safety guidance and whom to contact if the outage continues. Keep the plan useful, not elaborate: the point is to reduce searching when the lights are already out.
During the outage, resist the refrigerator peek

When the power fails, note the time if you can. Then leave both appliance doors shut. Each opening lets cold air escape, and a quick look rarely gives you the information you need about the food’s temperature. If the outage is brief, keeping the doors closed helps preserve the cold already inside. The CDC’s time guidance assumes the doors remain closed: up to four hours for a refrigerator, and about 48 hours for a full freezer or 24 hours for a half-full one. [1]

If you need something from the refrigerator, decide what you want before opening it and take it out quickly. Avoid moving food around just to inspect it. If the outage stretches on, use the time you noted and the appliance thermometers when it is appropriate to check, rather than relying on how cool the room feels or how cold a package seems to your hand. Those details can help you follow official guidance, but they do not replace it.
Agree on the handoffs, not just the supplies

A household plan works best when it names small, clear responsibilities. One person might note when power went out; another might know where the cooler and gel packs are; someone else might look up the official chart when power returns. These are options, not fixed roles. Choose them around who is present, who can safely do the task and who is comfortable using a phone or printed instructions.

Consider whose food needs require particular attention. A household may include a baby, an older adult, someone who is pregnant, or a person whose health makes foodborne illness especially concerning. Rather than trying to settle every special case from memory, decide in advance where you will find reliable advice and who will help check it. If someone may be away from home during an outage, make sure another trusted person can access the plan. The goal is a shared understanding, not a complicated emergency command structure.
When the power returns, use the chart

Restored electricity does not tell you whether food stayed cold enough. Start with how long the power was out, whether refrigerator doors stayed closed and any temperature information you have. The CDC says to discard refrigerated perishable food after four hours without power, and advises against tasting food to judge its safety. Smell, appearance and a small bite cannot reliably establish that food is safe. [1]

For decisions about individual items, use the FoodSafety.gov power-outage chart rather than applying one rule to everything in the refrigerator. It sorts foods into categories and gives discard guidance, which is more useful than trying to memorize a universal list. [2] If you cannot determine whether a food is safe, do not taste it as a test; consult the chart or discard it. This can be frustrating, especially when food is costly or hard to replace. But an uncertain item is not made safer by trying a little. Keep the chart bookmarked or print it so that finding it does not depend on a strong internet connection.
Treat the freezer as a separate decision

A freezer can hold its temperature longer than a refrigerator, but the contents and how full it is make a difference. The CDC gives approximate closed-door windows of 48 hours for a full freezer and 24 hours for a half-full freezer. [1] That helps set expectations, but it is not a substitute for checking the food-specific guidance after power returns.

FoodSafety.gov’s chart covers frozen items and explains when food may be refrozen. Use those item-by-item instructions alongside what you know about the outage and the food’s condition; do not assume that every thawed item has the same answer. [2] Refreezing guidance also should not be confused with a promise that quality will be unchanged. Keep the freezer closed during the outage, then work through the chart without rushing. If you are unsure about a particular product, use the official guidance rather than deciding by taste.
Plan for a longer outage without improvising

If the outage is likely to continue, a cooler can help keep selected food cold, provided it is packed with ice or frozen gel packs and kept at 40°F or below. USDA recommends using a cooler with ice or frozen gel packs when needed and maintaining that temperature. [3] Check the cooler with a thermometer if one is available; do not treat the cooler itself as proof that its contents are cold enough. Keep its lid closed as much as practical, too.

It may help to keep a modest supply of foods that do not depend on refrigeration, along with water and any utensils or can opener they require. Choose items your household will actually eat and can use safely. If you rely on backup power, follow the equipment’s safety instructions; do not improvise a setup indoors. A food plan is only one part of outage preparation, and it should not create a new hazard while trying to save groceries.
Set up the plan at the kitchen table

Use ten unhurried minutes to make the plan real. Together, locate the refrigerator and freezer thermometers, cooler, gel packs and a printed or saved copy of the FoodSafety.gov chart. Write down where each item lives and agree who will note the outage time and who will check the chart afterward. If someone else may need to help, ask whether they can find the supplies and guidance without being coached. Add a note about any household food needs that call for specific advice, and name a trusted person to contact if the usual decision-maker is away.

Then leave the doors shut and the plan where everyone can reach it. The useful test is not whether the list looks thorough; it is whether another person can follow it when the kitchen is dark and the situation is distracting.
